memory_update.text: CHEF should be prioritized in later Serenity layers as the cleanest US-listed specialty foodservice distributor tied directly to chef-driven restaurants and hospitality.
WEST is a plausible underfollowed second-order coffee/beverage supply-chain candidate in the USD 300M-1B range; verify foodservice mix, facility utilization, leverage, and customer wins.
FARM is a below-USD-300M speculative shadow candidate with unusually direct DSD route-density relevance but high liquidity, leverage, and execution-risk concerns.

Specialty distribution route density may show up less in restaurant brand tickers and more in distributor economics: customer retention, SKU breadth, delivery frequency, local density, specialty category expertise, and service/maintenance attachment.

Need a later pass for private or non-US competitors and acquired assets: regional distributors, coffee-service route operators, bakery/produce/protein distributors, and cash-and-carry wholesalers may be economically important but not directly investable.

CHEF should be carried forward as the cleanest public pure-play for specialty restaurant distribution; verify organic growth, acquisition dependence, leverage, specialty mix, and distribution-cost pressure.

WEST belongs in the underfollowed restaurant-supplier universe as a B2B coffee/tea/extract and beverage-capacity supplier, but must be tested for leverage, customer concentration, and whether new capacity earns adequate returns.

FARM is a speculative shadow candidate below the preferred market-cap threshold; its DSD coffee route network is node-relevant, but survival depends on liquidity, route profitability, and input-cost pass-through.
PFGC is useful as the reference benchmark for scale economics in foodservice, convenience, and specialty distribution, while CHEF/WEST/FARM better fit the underfollowed discovery lane.

Need a follow-up pass for non-distributor enablers: cold-chain fleet leasing, refrigeration equipment, warehouse automation, food-safety testing, route-optimization software, and packaging/dispensing equipment tied to specialty foodservice distribution.

CHEF is the cleanest underfollowed specialty-distribution candidate for the restaurant route-density node: specialty foods, center-of-the-plate products, chef/customer relationships, distribution centers, and delivery fleet.

WEST is a small-cap category-specialist candidate for coffee/tea/beverage supply into restaurants, foodservice, c-stores, hospitality, and travel centers; thesis depends on margin conversion and capacity utilization.

HFFG is a high-purity but below-USD-300M speculative exception for Asian restaurant distribution; next layers must heavily penalize governance, internal controls, losses, related-party exposure, and cash conversion if not improving.

Need a dedicated follow-up search for publicly listed route-based coffee DSD and bakery/produce/protein specialists; FARM appears highly relevant operationally but too small and financially distressed to rank as a core candidate without stronger evidence.

For this node, the key chokepoint variables are not brand power but route density, fill-rate reliability, cold-chain handling, category-specific sourcing, customer stickiness, labor/fuel pass-through, private-label or specialty mix, and acquisition integration discipline.

CHEF is the cleanest underfollowed public candidate for specialty restaurant foodservice distribution: upscale/higher-end dining, hard-to-find SKUs, center-of-plate proteins, sourcing, and logistics platform.
WEST should be tracked as a small-cap adjacent coffee/tea/beverage supply-chain candidate; exposure is plausible but requires channel mix and profitability verification.

HFFG is a micro-cap speculative exception with direct niche Asian-restaurant distribution exposure; financial quality, governance, margin stability, and liquidity must be verified before later-layer survival.

Restaurant distribution chokepoints may appear not only in broadline scale but also in specialty sourcing, category expertise, ethnic-foodservice networks, coffee/beverage solutions, and direct-store or dense-route delivery models.

Farmer Brothers was surfaced in external context as a coffee roaster/supplies distributor with direct-store-delivery relevance, but its approximately $28M market cap makes it a very small speculative shadow candidate; revisit only if the pass explicitly allows sub-$300M route businesses.
